summary: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a home address, a home agent address and a security association with the home agent before it can register. This informational document discusses the problems of obtaining that information, called bootstrapping, and several deployment scenarios in which it must happen.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a mobile device can use Mobile IPv6, it needs a permanent address, the address of its home agent, and credentials for secure communication with that agent. RFC 4640 describes this setup problem and the deployment situations a solution would need to handle.

subtitle: The setup information a mobile node needs before it can register with a Mobile IPv6 home agent.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 assumes a node already has a home address, home-agent address and security relationship with the home agent. Static provisioning of this information creates deployment difficulties.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4640 defines bootstrapping, describes provider roles and deployment scenarios, and identifies seed information for two cases depending on whether network-access and mobility authentication are independent.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a solution. It deliberately leaves preferred bootstrapping procedures to separate documents and excludes scenarios without a trust relationship to a provider.

facts.label: Information needed
facts.value: Home-agent address, home address and security association

today: RFC 4640 is an Informational problem statement, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. It says preferred bootstrapping solutions would be described in separate documents.

sections.title: What Bootstrapping Means
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 assumes that a mobile node has a trust relationship with a home agent and enough information to register. Bootstrapping is the process of obtaining the home address, home-agent address and security credentials needed for that registration.

A node may need to bootstrap when it starts without saved information, after a reboot, after a prefix change, or periodically to refresh credentials. The RFC defines the problem and lists minimal seed information for different deployment scenarios, but stops short of selecting a preferred solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Bootstrapping is the setup that gives a mobile device the information it needs to register with its home agent. The RFC describes what must be available, not the procedure that provides it.

sections.title: Goals and Non-Goals
sections.content:
At the end of bootstrapping, the node needs a home-agent address, a home address, and an IPsec security association between the node and the agent, including an IKE pre-shared secret. Bootstrapping may be started by the node or network, including to refresh credentials while the node is registered.

Exchanged configuration must have integrity and replay protection; confidentiality should be provided when needed. Home-prefix renumbering is not a specific goal, and bootstrapping without a trust relationship between the node and any provider is outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup must provide addresses and secret credentials, and it may be repeated when information needs refreshing. This document does not cover setup when the user has no trusted service provider.

sections.title: Why Static Provisioning Is Difficult
sections.content:
The RFC explains that the base Mobile IPv6 setup ties security policy to specific home addresses and home-agent addresses. Static entries make dynamic home-address or agent assignment difficult and can complicate network management when addresses or providers change.

The document also discusses integration with authentication, authorization and accounting infrastructure. It notes that dormant devices may miss pushed prefix changes, so they may need to bootstrap again when they return to service.
sections.plainLanguage: Entering addresses and security settings by hand makes changes difficult to manage. A device that was asleep during a network change may need to obtain its setup information again.

sections.title: Provider Roles and Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC separates network access service from mobility service. An access service provider (ASP) provides IP connectivity; a mobility service provider (MSP) provides Mobile IPv6 service. The organization that authorizes each service may be the provider itself or another organization.

It describes a mobility-service subscription, an integrated access and mobility provider, a third-party MSP, and an infrastructure-less scenario. The first three rely on an existing trust relationship; the infrastructure-less case is described but not supported by the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The company that provides Internet access may differ from the company that keeps a device reachable as it moves. A setup solution needs to account for these arrangements and who trusts whom.

sections.title: Seed Information and Security Risks
sections.content:
When network-access authentication is independent of mobility authentication, the node may need the home-agent domain name and IKE credentials. When the two authentications share a security association, network-access credentials can provide the seed information described by the RFC.

Threats include a false home-agent address, false security associations, stolen credentials and denial of service against a bootstrapping service. The RFC says keys for network access and mobility service must remain cryptographically separate, separately named and have separate lifetimes, even when they come from the same credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The initial information depends on whether the user signs in separately for Internet access and mobile reachability. The setup must protect credentials and keep the keys for those services separate.
